prompt:
Summarize the following passage in ONE sentence.

The town of Harlow's Bend installed a fleet of solar-powered streetlights last autumn, replacing the old sodium lamps that had flickered for two decades. Residents reported that the new lights were brighter and that their evening electricity bills dropped slightly because the lamps no longer drew from the municipal grid. The council estimated the project would pay for itself within seven years through energy savings.
expected: Harlow's Bend replaced its old streetlights with solar-powered ones that are brighter, cut grid electricity use, and are expected to pay for themselves within about seven years.
rubric: Mentions the switch to solar-powered streetlights
Notes a benefit (brighter and/or reduced electricity/grid use)
Is a single sentence

prompt:
What is the main idea of this paragraph? Answer in one or two sentences.

Many people believe that adding more lanes to a congested highway will reduce traffic. In practice, the opposite often happens. When a road is widened, driving becomes temporarily easier, which encourages more people to drive on it, until congestion returns to roughly its previous level. Transportation researchers call this effect 'induced demand.'
expected: Widening highways usually fails to relieve congestion because the added capacity induces more people to drive (induced demand), restoring the original level of traffic.
rubric: States that widening highways does not durably reduce congestion
Explains the cause: more capacity attracts more drivers (induced demand)

Please store enough drinking and washing water in advance. Elevators will continue to operate normally. The laundry room will be closed for the day. If the work finishes early, water service will be restored without further notice. For emergencies during the shutoff, call the building office at 555-0142.
expected: Water will be shut off building-wide on Thursday March 14 from 9 AM to about 4 PM to replace the corroded main riser; tenants should store water in advance; elevators run normally but the laundry room is closed; service may return early without notice; emergencies call 555-0142.
rubric: States the date (March 14) and time window (about 9 AM to 4 PM)
States the reason: replacing the corroded main riser
Advises storing water in advance
Notes laundry room closed (and/or elevators still working)
Includes the emergency contact number 555-0142

prompt:
Summarize the following passage in 2-3 sentences in your own words.

The Atacama Desert in northern Chile is one of the driest places on Earth; some weather stations there have never recorded rainfall. Yet the desert is far from lifeless. Specialized microbes survive by extracting moisture directly from the thin morning fog that rolls in from the Pacific. Because conditions in the Atacama resemble those on Mars, NASA has used the region as a testing ground for instruments designed to detect life on other planets. Studying how organisms endure such extreme dryness helps scientists understand the outer limits of where life can exist.
expected: The Atacama Desert is extremely dry yet hosts microbes that draw water from coastal fog. Because its conditions resemble Mars, NASA tests life-detection instruments there, and studying these organisms reveals the limits of where life can survive.
rubric: Captures that the Atacama is extremely dry but supports microbial life (fog-derived moisture)
Notes the Mars analogy / NASA testing of life-detection instruments
Mentions the scientific value: understanding limits of life
Is paraphrased, not copied verbatim

prompt:
Identify (a) the author's main claim and (b) the single piece of evidence they use to support it.

Four-day workweeks are not the productivity disaster critics feared. When a mid-sized software firm in Wellington trialed a four-day schedule with no reduction in pay, its managers tracked output across six months and found that completed project milestones actually rose by 8 percent compared with the prior year. Employees reported feeling less burned out, and turnover fell. The firm has since made the schedule permanent.
expected: (a) Claim: four-day workweeks do not hurt productivity (they can even help). (b) Evidence: a Wellington software firm's six-month trial showed completed project milestones rose 8% versus the prior year (with lower burnout/turnover).
rubric: States the main claim: four-day workweeks don't harm (or improve) productivity
Identifies the evidence: the Wellington firm's trial / 8% rise in completed milestones

prompt:
Trace the cause-and-effect chain described in the passage, in order, as a short ordered list.

An unusually warm winter meant the lake never froze over. Without ice cover, sunlight kept reaching the water all season, so algae continued to grow instead of dying back. The thick algae bloom then consumed much of the dissolved oxygen as it later decomposed. By spring, the low oxygen levels had suffocated a large portion of the lake's fish, and local anglers reported the worst season in memory.
expected: 1) A warm winter prevented the lake from freezing. 2) No ice meant sunlight kept reaching the water. 3) Algae kept growing (a bloom) instead of dying back. 4) The decomposing algae consumed dissolved oxygen. 5) Low oxygen suffocated many fish. 6) Anglers had their worst season.
rubric: Starts with warm winter -> no ice/no freeze
Connects sunlight reaching water -> continued algae growth/bloom
Connects decomposing algae -> oxygen depletion
Ends with low oxygen -> fish die-off (and poor angling)
Presents steps in correct causal order

prompt:
Summarize the following passage in 3-4 sentences, capturing both the discovery and its significance.

For decades, biologists assumed that the giant kelp forests off the Pacific coast were sustained almost entirely by sunlight and nutrients rising from deep water. A research team has now documented a surprising second source: the daily migration of millions of tiny crustaceans called krill. Each night the krill rise toward the surface to feed, and each morning they sink back into deeper water, carrying nutrients downward in their bodies and waste. The team calculated that this vertical 'conveyor belt' delivers nearly a fifth of the nitrogen the kelp depends on. Because warming oceans are already disrupting krill migration patterns, the finding raises concern that kelp forests could decline even in places where sunlight and upwelling remain unchanged. The researchers argue that conservation models must now account for these animal-driven nutrient flows rather than treating kelp ecosystems as purely sunlight-and-current driven.
expected: Researchers found that nightly vertical migrations of krill supply nearly a fifth of the nitrogen that Pacific kelp forests need, a source previously overlooked in favor of sunlight and upwelling. Because warming oceans disrupt krill migration, kelp forests could decline even where light and currents are unchanged. The authors conclude that conservation models must include animal-driven nutrient flows.
rubric: States the discovery: krill migration supplies a major share (~1/5) of kelp's nitrogen
Notes this source was previously overlooked / assumed to be sunlight+upwelling only
Captures the significance: warming disrupts krill, threatening kelp even where light/currents are fine
Notes the implication for conservation models (include animal-driven nutrient flows)

Critics have praised the architecture. Without question, it is the finest museum in the entire country, and anyone who disagrees simply doesn't understand art.
expected: Factual summary: The museum's new 12,000-square-foot wing opened in April, cost $14 million, and displays 340 loaned works that critics have praised. The opinion/unsupported claim is that it is 'the finest museum in the entire country' (and that dissenters don't understand art).
rubric: Summarizes the verifiable facts (size, cost, opening, number of works)
Correctly identifies the 'finest museum in the country' statement (and/or the dismissal of dissenters) as opinion rather than fact

prompt:
The passage presents two viewpoints. Summarize each side's position in one sentence, then state where they actually agree.

In the debate over the proposed bike-lane network, the Cyclists' Coalition argues that protected lanes will save lives, citing data showing that physically separated lanes cut cycling injuries dramatically; they say a few minutes of slower car traffic is a fair trade. The Merchants' Association counters that removing a lane of car traffic and dozens of parking spaces will choke deliveries and drive away customers who arrive by car, hurting small businesses. Notably, though, both groups have publicly stated they want more people visiting the downtown core and agree that the current intersection at Fifth and Main, where three serious crashes occurred last year, is dangerous and must be fixed.
expected: Cyclists' Coalition: protected bike lanes will reduce injuries and save lives, worth slightly slower car traffic. Merchants' Association: removing a car lane and parking will hurt deliveries and drive away car-arriving customers, harming small businesses. Both agree they want more visitors downtown and that the dangerous Fifth-and-Main intersection must be fixed.
rubric: Summarizes the Cyclists' Coalition view (protected lanes reduce injuries/save lives)
Summarizes the Merchants' Association view (lost lane/parking hurts deliveries and businesses)
Identifies the agreement: both want more downtown visitors and want the dangerous Fifth-and-Main intersection fixed

prompt:

A pilot program gave 150 unhoused individuals in a single city a no-strings monthly cash payment for one year. By the end, recipients were significantly more likely to have stable housing and reported lower stress than a comparison group that received only standard services. However, the authors caution that the sample was small, drawn from one city with an unusually tight rental market, and that the one-year window may be too short to know whether the gains last. They recommend a larger, multi-city trial running at least three years before any city scales the approach into permanent policy.
expected: The pilot found that unhoused recipients of a year of unconditional monthly cash were more likely to achieve stable housing and reported less stress than a comparison group. The authors caution the study was limited by a small, single-city sample with an unusual rental market and a possibly too-short one-year window. They recommend a larger, multi-city trial of at least three years before scaling the approach into policy.
rubric: States the result: cash recipients had more stable housing / lower stress vs. comparison group
States the acknowledged limitation (small/single-city sample, unusual market, or short one-year window)
States the recommendation: a larger multi-city, longer (3+ year) trial before scaling
Is three sentences

prompt:
In one clear sentence, state the central thesis of this dense paragraph, stripping away the supporting detail.

Proponents of measuring national success purely through gross domestic product overlook that the metric, by design, counts all market activity as a positive contribution while remaining blind to its distribution and its costs. A nation can post robust GDP growth even as that growth flows overwhelmingly to a narrow slice of the population, even as the activity generating it depletes finite resources or pollutes shared air and water, and even as unpaid labor such as caregiving, which sustains the very workforce the economy depends on, goes entirely uncounted. To treat GDP as a sufficient measure of a society's progress is therefore to mistake the volume of transactions for the health of the people conducting them.
expected: GDP is an inadequate measure of national progress because it counts all market activity as positive while ignoring inequality, environmental costs, and unpaid labor, thereby confusing economic activity with genuine societal well-being.
rubric: States that GDP is an inadequate/insufficient measure of progress or well-being
References at least one of its blind spots (distribution/inequality, environmental cost, or unpaid labor)
Is a single sentence capturing the thesis, not the supporting examples

prompt:
The passage contains an apparent contradiction. Summarize the passage in 2-3 sentences and explain how the contradiction is resolved.

The report says the company's profits fell last quarter, yet its stock price rose sharply the same week. At first glance this seems backwards. The explanation lies in expectations: analysts had predicted an even steeper drop in profits, so when the actual decline turned out to be milder than feared, investors treated the result as good news relative to what they had braced for, and they bought shares accordingly.
expected: Although the company's quarterly profits fell, its stock rose because analysts had expected an even larger decline; the actual, milder drop beat expectations, so investors saw it as relatively good news and bought shares. The contradiction is resolved by recognizing that stock prices react to results relative to expectations, not to the raw direction of profits.
rubric: States the apparent contradiction: profits fell yet the stock rose
Explains the resolution: the decline was smaller than analysts had feared (beat expectations)
Conveys that prices move on expectations relative to forecasts, not absolute results
